newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope tells China to respect Hong Kong Catholics.
newsitem.headline: Pope tells China to respect Hong Kong Catholics.

text.p: Pope John Paul told China on Monday the Vatican would be closely watching how Catholics in Hong Kong are treated after the British colony is handed over to Beijing this year.
The 76-year-old Pope made his comments in his annual "state of the world" address to diplomats accredited to the Vatican.
He also called for a redoubling of efforts to keep the Middle East peace process on track, and appealed for dialogue to end conflicts in Algeria, Cyprus, Sri Lanka and central Africa.

Turning his attention to Asia, the Pope told diplomats gathered in the Vatican's frescoed Sala Regia that the Holy See would be monitoring events in Hong Kong after the July 1 handover from Britain to Beijing.
"By reason of the size and vitality of the Catholic community in the territory, the Holy See will follow with very particular interest this new stage," he said.
The Pope was "trusting that respect for differences, for the fundamental rights of the human person and for the rule of law will accompany this new journey forward".
Last year the Pope appointed Shanghai-born Monsignor Joseph Zen, 64, as coadjudicator bishop of Hong Kong, which means he will eventually succceed Cardinal Joseph Wu as Catholic leader.

By appointing a bishop with right of succession before the handover, the Pope sought to guarantee continuity for the church in Hong Kong and effectively bypassed consultations with Beijing that would probably become necessary after July 1.

Beijing does not allow Catholics to recognise the Pope's authority. Chinese Catholics who want to worship openly must belong to the state-controlled Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association. Those loyal to the Pope worship secretly.

Beijing is bound to be upset on Tuesday when the Pope recieves Taiwan's Vice-President Lien Chan, the highest ranking Taiwanese official to visit the Vatican. Beijing wants the Vatican to sever ties with Taiwan.
The Pope dedicated a section of his address to the Mideast, saying everything must be done to ensure that past negotiations between Palestinians and Israelis will not have been in vain.

"All people together, Jews, Christians and Moslims, Israelis and Arabs, believers and non-believers, must create and reinforce peace: the peace of treaties, the peace of trust, the peace in people's hearts," he said.

If it was to endure, Middle East peace had to be based on dialogue that respected each side's identity, right of self determination, independence and security concerns, he said, adding: "There can be no exception."
The Palestinian representative to the Vatican, Afif Safieh, confirmed in a statement that President Yasser Arafat had invited the Pope last month to visit Bethlehem in the year 2000.

In other parts of his address the Pope said fundamentalist violence in Algeria had forced the country "to wallow in an abyss of unprecedented violence, giving a bleak impression of an entire people taken hostage."

In Africa, Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire "were trapped in the deadly cogs of unbridled violence and ethnic rivalry, which have plunged entire nations into human tragedies which should leave no one indifferent".
